name: Papilloedema
aliases: optic disc swelling from raised intracranial pressure

reference.source: Parsons' Diseases of the Eye / Kanski Clinical Ophthalmology
clinicalPearls: The term papilloedema refers specifically to optic disc swelling caused by raised intracranial pressure, and is characteristically bilateral
Central vision is often preserved early, while an enlarged blind spot and transient visual obscurations lasting seconds are typical

Accompanying symptoms of raised intracranial pressure include headache worse on waking or with Valsalva, nausea, vomiting, and pulsatile tinnitus, and a sixth nerve palsy may be a false localising sign

Fundus signs include blurred disc margins, hyperaemia, loss of the physiological cup, obscuration of vessels crossing the disc, and loss of spontaneous venous pulsation, with haemorrhages and cotton wool spots in more advanced cases
Idiopathic intracranial hypertension classically affects young women who are overweight, but a space-occupying lesion or venous sinus thrombosis must be excluded first
It must be distinguished from other causes of a swollen disc, such as optic neuritis, anterior ischaemic optic neuropathy, and pseudopapilloedema from optic disc drusen
Chronic untreated papilloedema leads to progressive optic atrophy and irreversible visual field loss
reference.pathophysiology: Papilloedema is passive swelling of the optic nerve head produced by raised intracranial pressure transmitted along the subarachnoid space surrounding the optic nerve. The elevated pressure impedes axoplasmic flow within the retinal ganglion cell axons at the optic disc, causing them to become distended, along with venous congestion and leakage that produce the characteristic disc appearance. Because the mechanism is mechanical rather than primarily ischaemic or inflammatory, central acuity is often spared until late. Persistently raised pressure eventually causes axonal loss and secondary optic atrophy.
additionalDifferentials: Optic neuritis (usually unilateral, with pain and reduced acuity)
Pseudopapilloedema from optic disc drusen or a crowded hypermetropic disc
Infiltrative or inflammatory optic disc swelling
additionalInvestigations: Urgent neuroimaging (MRI or CT with venography) to exclude a mass lesion or venous sinus thrombosis
Lumbar puncture with opening pressure and cerebrospinal fluid analysis once imaging excludes a mass
Visual field testing to detect an enlarged blind spot and peripheral loss
Blood pressure measurement to exclude malignant hypertension
Optical coherence tomography and fundus photography to grade and monitor disc swelling
Assessment of colour vision and pupils to help distinguish from optic neuropathies
redFlags: Bilateral disc swelling mandating urgent workup for raised intracranial pressure, including neuroimaging to exclude a tumour or venous sinus thrombosis
Progressive visual field loss or declining acuity indicating threatened optic nerve function
New focal neurological signs or a sixth nerve palsy
Very high intracranial or blood pressure requiring emergency management
reference.prognosis: Vision can be preserved if the underlying cause of raised intracranial pressure is treated promptly, but delayed or chronic papilloedema leads to optic atrophy and permanent visual field loss.
pitfalls: Mistaking pseudopapilloedema from disc drusen for true papilloedema and initiating unnecessary invasive workup
Diagnosing idiopathic intracranial hypertension before excluding a mass lesion or venous thrombosis
Reassuring the patient because central acuity is normal while field loss progresses
Overlooking malignant hypertension as a cause of disc swelling
management: Directed treatment of the underlying cause of raised intracranial pressure, such as resection of a mass lesion or anticoagulation for cerebral venous sinus thrombosis
In idiopathic intracranial hypertension, weight reduction combined with a carbonic anhydrase inhibitor such as acetazolamide as first-line medical therapy
Surgical intervention for medically refractory or vision-threatening disease, including cerebrospinal fluid shunting, optic nerve sheath fenestration or venous sinus stenting
Serial monitoring of optic nerve function with visual fields, optical coherence tomography and fundus assessment to detect progression to optic atrophy
Prompt neuroimaging with venography to exclude a mass or venous thrombosis before any lumbar puncture
Joint ophthalmology and neurology or neurosurgery management, with urgent referral when vision is threatened
